implementation_notes: The Observer/Subject class hierarchy collapses into std::function targets stored in a std::vector: subscribe pushes a lambda (or a std::bind of a member function), notify iterates and calls each target, unsubscribe erases by id. The class-based form is only worth it when observers must be polymorphic across a boundary or must expose more than the update operation. std::function copies the callable, so capture by value or through std::weak_ptr/std::reference_wrapper - a lambda capturing a raw this dangles as soon as the observer is destroyed.
pitfalls: A lambda capturing this keeps a dangling pointer after the observer dies; capture a weak_ptr/observer_ref or unsubscribe in the observer's destructor.
Notifying while a handler subscribes or unsubscribes invalidates the vector's iterators and references - iterate over a copy or defer the mutation.
std::function copies the callable, so state captured by value is per-subscription; capture a pointer or std::reference_wrapper when the observer's own state must be shared.
The registry has no locking: concurrent subscribe/notify needs an external mutex, and holding that mutex while calling targets lets a handler deadlock by subscribing.

variants.name: Boost.Signals2 signal/slot (managed connections)
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Signals2 supplies the entire structure: signal<> is the subject, connect() returns a connection (or scoped_connection for RAII unsubscribe), slots may be tracked objects so the connection is dropped automatically when either end dies, and the library is the thread-safe successor of Boost.Signals. Prefer it when connection lifetime management, slot-ordering groups or return-value combiners matter; use the std::function registry for one or two local callbacks.
pitfalls: A lambda that captures this is not a tracked object: the connection only disappears when the scoped_connection member is destroyed, so declare it before (and destroy it after) the data it uses.
Signals2 is thread-safe for connect/disconnect and emission, but the slot body still runs in the emitting thread; the observer's own state needs its own synchronisation.
Choosing non-void slot returns changes the signal's semantics: results are combined by a combiner, and a mis-specified combiner silently discards all but one.
